one_line: Hookdeck's founder explains why he built an event gateway and the open-source Outpost to replace fragile webhook handling with queuing, replay, push-based rate control and per-vendor latency monitoring. Substantive but vendor-led.
summary: Better Stack podcast episode with Alex, founder of Hookdeck, and hosts Andrus and James. Alex traces Hookdeck's origin to frustration with webhooks while running e-commerce systems, and argues that webhooks are the entry point to event-driven architecture, where ordering, idempotency and delivery guarantees matter. He describes the Event Gateway (a managed endpoint that receives untrusted inbound events and then filters, transforms, routes, queues and replays them) and Outpost, an Apache 2.0 publisher-side project that also has a managed version running the same Docker image. A large part of the talk covers operating against vendors: they enforce short timeouts, so processing must be queued, and outages cause backlog floods on recovery. Hookdeck's Radar product tracks per-vendor delivery latency baselines, which exposes slowdowns that the receiver's own metrics miss. Alex also makes a case for push-based queues over pull-based consumers, and says LLM agents are creating new event sources and new capacity problems. The episode is a product-adjacent conversation with the founder, so self-reported figures (citation rate, subscriber counts, adoption) should be treated as unverified.

key_ideas.idea: Hookdeck has two products. The Event Gateway is a managed inbound endpoint that receives events from outside your infrastructure and then filters, transforms, routes, queues and replays them. Outpost is an Apache 2.0 publisher-side project that sends events to tenant endpoints or message buses, and it also has a managed version.
key_ideas.detail: Positioned as covering both sides of the interoperability problem: receiving vendor webhooks in one contract, and publishing events to customers over webhooks or directly to queues such as Kafka, RabbitMQ, SQS, Pub/Sub and EventBridge.

key_ideas.idea: The company started from frustration with webhooks while running e-commerce systems. Each webhook needed retries, a dead-letter path, replay and per-vendor quirks, and none of that came packaged.
key_ideas.detail: Alex first published a Medium post on the topic and built a prototype in his basement. The early approach focused on visibility, which did not solve the underlying problem.

key_ideas.idea: A webhook is only the transport. Behind every webhook is an event, and handling it at serious scale brings in event-driven concerns such as idempotency, ordering and delivery guarantees, so the product grew into a full queue.
key_ideas.detail: This is the argument for saying 'event' rather than 'webhook', and for calling webhooks the gateway drug into event-driven architecture. The speaker also concedes that some of the complexity is real and cannot be fully abstracted away.

key_ideas.idea: The gateway works over plain HTTP. You swap your vendor-facing webhook URL for the gateway URL, and the gateway pushes events to your endpoint at a configured rate, so no code change or redeploy is needed and it works on any stack.
key_ideas.detail: Contrasted with AWS EventBridge, where the vendor must integrate with AWS. The speaker says EventBridge has roughly 40 vendor integrations, hedged with 'don't quote me'.

key_ideas.idea: Vendors enforce short response timeouts, often 3 to 5 seconds, so real processing must be queued and handled asynchronously. After an outage, vendors drain their backlog at high rates, which produces traffic spikes that the receiver must autoscale for.
key_ideas.detail: Slow responses also hurt the sender: connections stay open, so throughput falls, and vendors eventually disable the endpoint and events are lost. Keeping response times healthy is partly outside the receiver's control.

key_ideas.idea: Radar aggregates delivery latency per vendor across customers and alerts when it drifts from its baseline. Latency creep, such as delivery delays rising from about 5 seconds toward 60 seconds, is hard to see in your own metrics and can break time assumptions in business logic.
key_ideas.detail: Shopify's baseline is cited at about 4 to 5 seconds, with alerts beyond about 10 seconds. A significant latency incident happens roughly every two months. The goal is to tell 'is it me or my vendor' with data, while the speaker cautions against blaming vendors too quickly.

key_ideas.idea: Push-based queues are preferred over per-queue polling consumers. Polling needs one consumer per queue, which multiplies with per-customer or per-topic queues, while push lets many queues feed one horizontally scaled endpoint and keeps throughput control in the queue.
key_ideas.detail: Pub/Sub push mode is criticised for a sawtooth pattern: it ramps the send rate until the receiver slows, then backs off to near zero and repeats. Fine-grained rate control is presented as the reason push simplifies architecture.

key_ideas.idea: The term 'event gateway' was coined to sit between an event bus and an API gateway. It has since been adopted by Kong and others, and the speaker says LLMs cite Hookdeck in about 60 percent of relevant prompts.
key_ideas.detail: Self-reported. The speaker frames a shared category vocabulary as useful for customers, even if the terminology converges over time.

key_ideas.idea: Agents are becoming event consumers. Their runs are non-deterministic and can be long, which makes capacity, backpressure, timeouts and failure rates harder to manage than with short deterministic handlers.
key_ideas.detail: Examples include GitHub PR and comment events, support tickets and sensor data. Agents also trigger other agents, so agent outputs become events. The speaker argues event destinations are a better pattern than webhooks for this.

key_ideas.idea: Open source as a business choice: the managed Outpost runs the same Docker image as the open-source project, with no private fork. Feature requests are routed to GitHub issues and PRs, which turns managed users into contributors, but AI-written PRs now add review load.
key_ideas.detail: One open PR adds Cloudflare Queues as a destination using APIs that appear not to exist, which shows the cost of unreviewed agent-written contributions. The team still has to decide whether to act on such requests.

techniques.name: Push-based webhook intake in front of your endpoint
techniques.how: Point each vendor's webhook at a gateway URL instead of your own, then configure the gateway destination as your existing endpoint. The gateway accepts the request, queues it, and delivers to your endpoint at a rate you set. This needs no change to your code and works on any cloud or stack.
techniques.when: When vendor timeouts or spikes make synchronous handling unreliable and you cannot or will not redeploy the consumer.

techniques.name: Respond fast, queue the work
techniques.how: Do not perform business processing inside the webhook handler. Acknowledge the vendor request immediately, enqueue the event, and process it asynchronously.
techniques.when: Whenever vendors enforce 3 to 5 second timeouts or send bursts after their own outages.

techniques.name: Per-vendor delivery latency baseline and alerting
techniques.how: Track delivery latency per vendor over time (the speaker uses p99 and uptime), establish a baseline, and alert when latency moves several standard deviations above it. Use this data to separate vendor-side delay from your own processing delay.
techniques.when: When delays cause incorrect business behavior that your own HTTP and tracing metrics do not show, such as slow arrival rather than failure.

techniques.name: Per-tenant queues with a shared push consumer
techniques.how: Create one queue per tenant, topic or condition, and push all of them to one autoscaled, load-balanced consumer API. Rate control stays on the queue side, not in the consumer.
techniques.when: When a noisy tenant must not block others, and running one consumer per queue would multiply workers.

techniques.name: Event destinations instead of HTTP webhook transport
techniques.how: Publish events directly to the destination's native bus, such as Kafka, RabbitMQ, SQS, Pub/Sub or EventBridge, rather than sending HTTP webhooks.
techniques.when: When the downstream consumer already runs on a message queue and HTTP adds latency, security or efficiency costs.

techniques.name: Open-source-first with a managed twin
techniques.how: Ship the managed service from the identical open-source Docker image, with no private fork. Route feature requests to existing issues or PRs and point users to the repository so they can contribute.
techniques.when: When you want to avoid open-core incentive conflicts and reduce the barrier for contributors.

techniques.name: Verify agent-written contributions against real APIs
techniques.how: Check that every external API a PR relies on exists and matches current documentation before weighing its merit. The speaker describes a PR whose description looked plausible but whose code called APIs that do not exist.
techniques.when: When reviewing contributions from coding agents or unknown contributors.

numbers.claim: Vendor response timeouts are typically around 3 to 5 seconds.
Shopify delivery latency baseline is about 4 to 5 seconds; Radar alerts above about 10 seconds.
Latency can creep to around 60 seconds without showing as a downtime event.
A significant Shopify latency incident occurs roughly once every two months.
The Shopify Radar monitor has a couple hundred subscribers.
EventBridge has about 40 vendor integrations (speaker hedges, 'don't quote me').
Hookdeck is cited in about 60 percent of LLM responses to webhook and event gateway prompts (self-reported).
Hookdeck has about 10 people, and has worked with hundreds of thousands of developers.
A pre-seed of about 400k USD came from angel investors before a Hacker News launch.
A Railway GCP account shutdown took one of the hosted Outpost free-plan instances down for about 6 hours.

hot_takes: Pull-based message queues are 'very dumb' compared with push-based queues, and no mainstream queue gets push right because throughput control is pushed into consumers.
Webhooks are the gateway drug into event-driven architecture, and the term 'event' is preferred over 'webhook'.
LLM agents are a new source of event volume, since they are triggered by events and need to emit events, so webhook traffic will grow.
Code review and security scanning are table stakes. Taste, customer understanding and judgment about what is worth building still add the value, and LLM-generated output does not supply them.
Vendor blame is too easy. Teams should verify latency with their own data before attributing slowness to a vendor.
Caveat: this is a founder-led conversation about a product the speaker sells, so adoption and citation figures are self-reported and the technical claims about queues are opinion.

relevance.why: Event-triggered agent workloads with non-deterministic, long runs need backpressure and per-tenant queuing. This overlaps with the 4-class priority scheduler and the Govrix proxy budgets, but the talk is not about LLM inference or agent memory.
relevance.action: Read the agentic-events segment around 37:55 and compare its backpressure and capacity concerns with the InferCraft priority scheduler before designing an event-triggered agent path.

relevance.why: Loops and schedules that respond to external events, and long-running non-deterministic agent runs, raise the same capacity and backpressure concerns. The talk offers no concrete harness design.
relevance.action: When designing ProsHarness loops triggered by external events, queue the events rather than handling them synchronously, and set a rate limit per run, using the timeout and backpressure points at 33:02 and 37:55 as the design check.
